PAPER: Production Engineering (2026) 20:27 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11740-025-01412-4 ORIGINAL PAPER Why the quantification of modularity effects remains an issue for modular product families Jakob Meinertz Grønvald1 · Morten Nørgaard1 · Carsten Keinicke Fjord Christensen1 · Niels Henrik Mortensen1 · Alberto Urueña2 Received: 25 April 2025 / Accepted: 15 December 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract This study examines the challenges regarding the quantification of modularity effects, focusing on data quality, availability, and management practices within four industrial production companies in Denmark. While the literature identifies many effects of modularity, a substantial gap persists regarding data availability and quality for accurate and practical quantifica- tion. This study reveals that less than half of the modularity-related effects have sufficient data for analysis. Furthermore, critical data such as bill-of-material have observed frequent inconsistencies with far-reaching consequences that further undermine data reliability. Silo effects also hinder knowledge sharing and limit holistic assessments of modularity effects. Traditional cost accounting methods often overlook indirect costs, leading to underestimations of modularity’s economic impact, while this study finds that even direct costs lack accuracy and consistency. The results in this paper imply that the Danish industry, and likely other sectors too, may benefit from more rigorous data practices, including tracking time expenditures in overhead departments, to facilitate modularity quantification. Future research may include how accounting systems impact data management, developing structured data management frameworks, including artificial intelligence, to enhance data quality, improve quantifiability, and encourage knowledge sharing within and across departments. Ultimately, these advancements would support informed, data-driven decisions regarding modular product development and support bridging the gap between research and successful industrial application. JSON: Name: time_driven_modularity_quant_pipeline Title: A time-driven activity-based costing and cross-system data reconciliation pipeline to increase the quantitative measurability of modularity effects in modular product families Short Hypothesis: Deploying a pipeline that combines time-driven activity-based costing, cross-system bill-of-material reconciliation, and AI-assisted entity matching increases the proportion of modularity-related effects that can be quantified from under 50% to at least 80% within 12 months in participating companies. Related Work: Existing approaches to quantify modularity effects fall into three categories: (1) traditional cost-accounting and ERP-driven allocations that provide reliable direct cost data but systematically under-allocate or evenly spread indirect/overhead costs across products; (2) activity-based costing (ABC) and time-driven ABC variants that improve overhead allocation granularity but require disciplined time-tracking and cross-system identifiers which are rarely present in practice; and (3) conceptual/decision-support frameworks (e.g., impact models, platform-assessment matrices, product commonality/generational indices) that enumerate many modularity effects but rely on qualitative scoring or expert judgment and lack robust, transferable measurement mappings. Separately, recent proposals use point solutions such as break-even analyses for inventory or AI methods for entity matching in BOMs, but these either address a single effect class or assume high-quality linked data. The main unresolved issues are (a) pervasive data quality and identifier inconsistencies across ERP/CAD/configurator systems, (b) lack of observed time-usage data in overhead functions, and (c) limited evidence that ABC-like methods can be operationalized in SME settings to yield broad, verifiable quantification of modularity effects. Abstract: Quantifying the economic effects of product modularity is impeded by fragmented data, inconsistent bills of materials, siloed systems, and absent time-usage records for overhead activities. This research proposes a structured, operational pipeline that combines (i) cross-system identifier reconciliation and BOM consistency checks, (ii) AI-assisted entity resolution to unify items and assemblies across ERP/CAD/configurator sources, and (iii) time-driven activity-based costing (TD-ABC) procedures deployed in sales, engineering, procurement, and service to capture overhead resource use. The main contribution is an end-to-end, reproducible research pipeline that translates previously qualitative modularity effects into measurable KPIs and monetary estimates. The pipeline will be validated on industrial datasets from modular product firms by measuring the increase in the share of modularity effects that are quantifiable, the accuracy of reconciled BOMs, and the reduction in overhead allocation error. Expected outcomes include an evidence-based evaluation of which modularity effects become tractable with pragmatic data practices and a benchmark for implementing TD-ABC and reconciliation in SME contexts. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Industrial datasets from four participating companies: ERP purchase/order tables, CAD part lists, production BOMs, sales configurator logs, service/spare-parts records, and historical sales/orders (project-level). (2) Synthetic benchmark datasets derived from real schemas with controlled noise levels for identifier mismatches, missing fields, and BOM structural variants. Baselines: (A) current practice (ERP direct-cost allocations + even overhead distribution), (B) standard ABC without time-driven inputs (activity mapping from records), (C) AI-BOM reconciliation only (entity matching without TD-ABC), (D) qualitative IMF scoring. Metrics: (1) Quantifiability rate = percentage of identified modularity effects for which required input data are present and usable for KPI calculation. (2) BOM reconciliation quality: precision, recall, F1 on matched item pairs against ground truth. (3) Overhead allocation error: RMSE and MAE of allocated overhead per order versus ground-truth time-tracking allocation. (4) Economic impact variance: relative change (%) in estimated modularity economic effect compared to baseline. (5) Time-to-evaluate: median time to produce a full modularity-effect evaluation for a product family. Experimental setup: (i) Install reconciliation module and AI entity matcher; run on historical datasets and synthetic benchmarks to measure BOM match metrics; (ii) Deploy TD-ABC time-tracking for sales/engineering/procurement/service in each company for 12 months and collect activity timestamps and durations; (iii) Run full pipeline to compute KPIs and monetary estimates of modularity effects; (iv) Compare results to baselines (A-D). Ablations: (1) full pipeline vs pipeline without AI entity matching; (2) full pipeline vs pipeline without TD-ABC (use activity proxies); (3) full pipeline with reduced reconciliation scope (only ERP↔production). Statistical analysis: paired comparisons (pre/post) per company, bootstrap CIs for quantifiability rate, significance testing with Wilcoxon signed-rank for nonparametric measures. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: AI-assisted entity matching may produce false merges/splits on items with minimal attribute overlap, degrading downstream KPI validity; BOM structural heterogeneity may exceed reconciliation model capacity. Data and adoption risks: inconsistent or incomplete historical records, refusal or low compliance with time-tracking in overhead departments, and privacy or contractual constraints on sharing cross-departmental records. Evaluation biases: small sample sizes and low-order volumes in SMEs reduce statistical power and can bias learning-curve or overhead estimates; results may overfit the participating companies' IT landscapes. Scalability and compute: reconciliation and ML training on large cross-linked industrial schemas can require substantial compute and tuning, limiting real-time operation. Generalization limits: pipeline validated on engineer-to-order and MTO/CTO settings may not generalize to high-volume discrete manufacturing or services without reconfiguration. Causality limits: increased quantifiability does not guarantee unbiased or accurate economic estimates; improved measurement may still leave systematic allocation biases unresolvable without organizational changes.
